title: Pictures of the Trinity
hookLine: the sun, its light and heat; a lover, a beloved, and love: every picture helps and falls short

cards: A small green plant, three leaves on one stem. A story people tell says Saint Patrick, preaching in Ireland, bent down, picked a shamrock, and held it up: three leaves, one plant. Whether it happened, nobody can show.
But the story keeps getting told, because it answers a real need. Christians say God is one, and God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and sooner or later somebody asks, how does that work?
And somebody reaches for a picture. Today: pictures of the Trinity.

teach.h: IN THE NAME: ONE NAME, THREE.
teach.b: Day two hundred ninety-nine called the Trinity one God in three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The Bible doesn't give a diagram, but it keeps naming the three together.
Jesus sends his friends out "baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." In the name. One name, three.
Paul ends a letter: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all." So teachers reached for pictures.

teach.h: THE SUN, ITS LIGHT, ITS WARMTH.
teach.b: One is the sun: the sun itself, its light, and the warmth that reaches your face. One sun, not three, and you never meet the light without the sun.
Augustine reached for love, which needs someone who loves, someone who is loved, and the love between them: three, and one act of love. And there's Patrick's shamrock.
Every one helps, and every one falls short. The sun can make the Son and the Spirit sound like products of the Father, less than him. The shamrock can make each person sound like a third of God.
A popular picture, water as ice, liquid and steam, can make God sound like one person changing costumes, which the creeds reject.
The old creed named after Athanasius warns against both mistakes: don't mix up the persons, and don't split the one God into pieces. So teachers keep using pictures, and keep letting them go.
It's the way of not-knowing again: a picture opens the door, and then you walk past it.

how: Christians baptize in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and teachers often use pictures like the sun or a shamrock to explain the Trinity, while saying that no picture is the reality.

games.q: what does “pictures of the trinity” mean?
o: images like a shamrock or the sun, each falling short
church windows that show only God the Father
paintings of three gods standing side by side

games.q: pictures and what they show — tap the pairs.
p: the sun, its light, its warmth
a lover, a beloved, and love
in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Ghost

s: in the King James text, Jesus says baptize in the names, plural
it says "in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost": one name, three.
the water picture, ice, liquid and steam, gets the Trinity exactly right
it can make God sound like one person changing costumes, which the creeds reject.
Augustine pictured the Trinity through love
someone who loves, someone who is loved, and the love between them.

games.q: a friend asks you to explain the Trinity, and you reach for water as ice, liquid and steam. what's the risk?
o: it makes God sound like one person changing costumes.
it makes God sound too small to see.
games.why: the creed named after Athanasius warns against mixing up the persons. every picture helps, and every picture falls short.

practice: Draw three overlapping circles, on paper, with a finger on the table, or in your mind, with one small shape in the middle where all three meet.
Look at the middle, then at where the picture breaks: circles have edges, and Christians say God doesn't. Let the drawing help and fall short at once; if you pray, you can pray toward the middle.

wordCard.voice: Pictures of the Trinity. The sun and its light and warmth; a lover, a beloved and love; a shamrock. Each opens a door, and none is the room.

orig.note: Greek: a set of three; the word Greek-speaking Christians used for the Trinity.

carryVoice: Your line: every picture falls short. Each one still opens a door. Rest well.
